definition: A brief summary at the beginning of a research paper outlining the study's purpose, methods, results and conclusions.
Measuring sleep and activity with a motion sensor worn on the wrist. It is more objective than asking people how well they slept.

Keeping people in a study unaware of who receives which treatment, so that expectations cannot sway the results. In a single-blind study the participants do not know; in a double-blind study neither the participants nor the researchers assessing them know.
Presenting only the results or studies that support a claim while leaving out those that do not.
A reference to another study or source, showing where information came from and allowing readers to verify claims.
An observational study that follows a group of people over time, sometimes for decades, to see how their habits or circumstances relate to later outcomes such as illness.
When researchers have financial, professional or personal interests that could influence their work. Good studies declare these transparently.
A third factor that influences both the supposed cause and the outcome, creating a link between them that is not causal. For example, wealth may explain why people who buy organic food are healthier.
A comparison group that doesn't receive the treatment being tested, used to determine if an intervention actually works.
Correlation means two things happen together; causation means one causes the other. Correlation does NOT prove causation.
An observational study that measures people once, at a single point in time. It can show that two things go together but not which came first.
The information collected during a study, which can include measurements, observations, survey responses or other recorded facts.
How large a difference or relationship is, not just whether there is one. For the common measure Cohen's d, about 0.2 counts as small, 0.5 as medium and 0.8 as large.
How much the results of the studies in a review or meta-analysis differ from one another. When it is high, a single pooled figure should be read with caution.
A testable prediction about what will happen in a study, based on existing knowledge or theory.
The average number of times a journal's recent articles are cited by other research. It is a rough sign of a journal's prestige but says little about the quality of any single study.
A statistical method that pools the results of several studies on the same question into one overall estimate. It is often part of a systematic review.
The section describing how the study was conducted, including participants, materials, procedures and analysis techniques.
A study in which researchers record what people already do or experience, without assigning them to groups. It can reveal associations but cannot by itself show cause and effect.
Research papers that are freely available to read online without a paywall or subscription. Anyone can access the full text immediately.
When researchers make their raw data publicly available so others can verify results and conduct their own analyses.
A free online platform where researchers can preregister studies and share their data, code and materials so that others can check and reuse them.
Trying many different analyses and reporting only those that reach statistical significance. It makes chance findings look real; preregistration helps to prevent it.
A barrier that requires payment (often £30+) or institutional access to read a research paper. This limits who can verify the science.
A process where other experts in the field evaluate a research paper before publication to check its quality and validity.

A dummy treatment, such as a sugar pill or a sham device, that looks like the real one but has no active ingredient. Comparing a treatment with a placebo shows whether it works beyond people's expectations (the placebo effect).

A publication that charges authors fees but skips proper peer review. Many reputable open-access journals also charge publication fees; the warning sign is the missing quality control. These journals prioritise profit over scientific quality.
An early version of a research paper shared publicly before peer review. Useful for rapid communication but not yet vetted by experts.
Declaring your research plan and analysis methods publicly before collecting data, which reduces bias and questionable research practices.

An experiment in which chance decides whether each participant receives the treatment being tested or joins a control group. Because the groups start out alike, differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.
Repeating a study to see if the same results occur. Replicable findings are more trustworthy than one-off results.
The section presenting what the study found, including statistical outcomes and data visualisations.
When the supposed effect is actually the cause. For example, people who sleep badly may use their phones more because they are awake, rather than phone use causing poor sleep.
The number of participants (N) or observations in a study. Larger samples generally provide more reliable results.

A finding is called statistically significant when results at least this strong would rarely occur by chance if there were really no effect (by convention, p < 0.05). It does not show how large or important an effect is, and a non-significant result does not prove that there is no effect.

A review that searches for all the studies on a question using a method set out in advance, assesses their quality and summarises the evidence. Unlike a narrative review, it is designed to avoid cherry-picking.

In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation of how something works, supported by evidence from many studies; in everyday speech the word often just means a guess. The rubric's Theory criterion asks something different: how well a study builds on existing research and whether it addresses a real gap in knowledge.
Any factor that can change or be measured in a study, such as age, temperature or test scores.
A report published directly by a company, industry body or campaign group, usually without independent peer review. White papers are often used for marketing or lobbying.
